title: Social Construction of Technology
body:
**Social construction of technology**, abbreviated SCOT, holds that social groups shape which
technologies get built and which succeed. Technical merit alone does not decide the outcome,
and the winner is frequently the option backed by the group with more influence.

The standard examples are historical. The bicycle went through decades of competing designs,
with the high-wheeled version favoured by young men seeking speed and the safety bicycle
favoured by everyone else, and the latter won because the relevant social group expanded. The
keyboard layout in use was settled by a mechanical constraint that stopped applying a century
ago. Videotape formats were decided by content availability, with the better picture losing.

The method is to identify the relevant social groups for a technology, describe what each
wanted from it, and trace how the disagreement closed. Closure happens when the debate stops,
and the best option winning is a separate event that may or may not coincide with it.

Applied to current systems the framework asks who is in the room when a design is settled. A
platform's moderation rules, a model's training data and a device's default settings all encode
the interests of whoever specified them, which is what makes the framework useful for
[[Ethical Analysis]] on a current system.

[[Technological Determinism]] is the opposing position.
